units.title: Mechanics of ventilation
units.summary: ● Inspiratory muscles ● Intrapulmonary volume ○ Diaphragm & intercostal muscles ○ Lung volume ○ Alveolar volume ○ Contract to induce inspiration ● Intrapulmonary pressure (P alv ) ○ Relax to induce expiration ○ Pressure in the alveoli ○ When it is higher than P atm, air flows ● Thoracic cavity out of lungs ○ Chest cavity ○ The chamber that encloses by chest ○ When it is lower than P atm, air flows wall (ribs, sternum and intercostal into lungs muscles) and diaphragm ● Atmospheric pressure (P atm ) ○ Include pleural cavity, lungs, heart, and other organs ○ At sea level, is ~760 mmHg (=1 atm) ○ Count as Zero in respiration process Inspiration Inspiratory muscles contract (diaphragm descends; rib cage rises). Intrapulmonary pressure drops to -1 mmHg. Air flows into lungs down the pressure gradient until intrapulmonary pressure is 0. Expiration Inspiratory muscles relax (diaphragm rises; rib cage descends due to recoil of costal cartilages).

Inspiration Inspiratory muscles contract (diaphragm descends; rib cage rises).
Intrapulmonary pressure drops to -1 mmHg.
Air flows into lungs down the pressure gradient until intrapulmonary pressure is 0.
Expiration Inspiratory muscles relax (diaphragm rises; rib cage descends due to recoil of costal cartilages).

units.title: Respiratory volumes, capacities, and ventilation
units.summary: Mechanics of Breathing • Several respiratory volumes can be used to assess status of pulmonary ventilation • Respiratory volumes can be combined to calculate respiratory capacities, which can give information on a person’s respiratory status • Respiratory volumes and capacities are usually abnormal in people with pulmonary disorders • Spirometer: original clinical tool used to measure patient’s respiratory volumes • Electronic measuring devices used today Average Value (Adult) Name Description Male Female Mechanics of Breathing • Anatomical dead space • Volume of air that does not take part in gas exchange • Consists of air that remains in conducting zone • Average 150 ml out of 500 ml TV • Alveolar dead space • Should be zero in healthy person • Space occupied by nonfunctional alveoli • Can be due to collapse or obstruction • Total dead space • sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space Mechanics of Breathing • Pulmonary Function Test • Spirometry can distinguish • Obstructive pulmonary disease: increased airway resistance (example: bronchitis) • TLC, FRC, RV may increase TLC • Restrictive disease: reduced TLC due to disease (example: tuberculosis) or exposure to environmental agents (example: fibrosis) TLC • VC, TLC, FRC, RV decrease because lung expansion is compromised Mechanics of Breathing • Pulmonary Function Test ○ Forced vital capacity (FVC) ■ amount of gas forcibly expelled after taking deep breath ○ Forced expiratory volume (FEV) ■ amount of gas expelled during specific time interval of FVC FVC ■ FEV 1: amount of air expelled in 1st second ○ Healthy individuals can expel 80% of FVC in 1st second ○ Patients with obstructive disease exhale less than 80% in 1st second ○ Patients with restrictive disease exhale 80% or more even with reduced FVC

units.title: Gas exchange between the lungs and blood
units.summary: Gas Exchange between Lungs and Blood • “Blue” in this figure • Deoxygenated blood containing less O 2 and more CO 2 • “Red” in this figure • Oxygenated blood containing more O 2 and less CO 2 • Gaseous exchange in lungs • O 2 up-taking: O 2 diffuse from alveoli to blood • CO 2 unloading: CO 2 diffuse from blood to alveoli Gas Exchange between Lungs and Blood • Partial pressures and gas concentrations • (1) The pressure exerted by each gas (Partial Pressure) in a mixture of gases is directly proportional to the percentage of the gas in the mixture. 21% O 2 & 760 mmHg • P O2 = 160 mmHg • (2) When a mixture of gases dissolves in liquid, the concentration of each gas in the liquid will be directly proportional to its partial pressure. higher partial pressure ⇒ higher concentration • partial pressure gradient ⇒ concentration gradient • When gas diffuse across the respiratory membrane • Region of higher partial pressure → Region of lower partial pressure • Down the partial pressure gradient!!! 160 mmHg 104 mmHg 0.3 mmHg 40 mmHg 40 mmHg 100 mmHg

units.title: Control of breathing
units.summary: Control of Breathing • Respiratory rhythms are regulated by voluntary and involuntary control mechanisms • Voluntary control of breathing • Human can exert conscious control over the rate and depth of our breathing. • The cerebral motor cortex send signals to motor neurons that control the respiratory muscles. • The respiratory centers in brainstem are bypassed. • However, the ability of holding breathe voluntarily is limited. Control of Breathing • Involuntary control of breathing • Respiratory centers in brainstem • Motor neurons from respiratory centers in brainstem transmit neural signals to affect contraction of respiratory muscles.
summary_sentences: Control of Breathing • Respiratory rhythms are regulated by voluntary and involuntary control mechanisms • Voluntary control of breathing • Human can exert conscious control over the rate and depth of our breathing.
• The cerebral motor cortex send signals to motor neurons that control the respiratory muscles.
• The respiratory centers in brainstem are bypassed.
• However, the ability of holding breathe voluntarily is limited.
